summary: Defines a framework for centralized conferencing, where participants on call signaling protocols such as SIP, H.323, or ISUP exchange media in a centralized unicast conference. It defines logical entities, naming, and the set of protocols that fit around them. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: A conference call with several people at once needs a server in the middle that mixes everyone's audio and video and keeps track of who is present. This RFC describes what that server and the pieces around it should look like, and what data they exchange.

questions: what is a sidebar in conferencing
subtitle: A framework for building multiparty voice and video conferences with one central server.

tldr.problem: Participants joining a conference from different kinds of phone and client need a common way to describe the conference, to control it, and to be told what is happening in it.
tldr.mechanism: The framework defines a conference object holding the data about a conference, a focus that holds a separate signalling session with each participant, and four protocols for signalling, notification, conference control and floor control.
tldr.outcome: A conferencing system can be built from these parts without the parts having to match between vendors. The RFC sets out the model and points to separate documents for the concrete protocols.

sections.title: A Framework for Centralized Conferencing
sections.content:
This document defines the framework for Centralized Conferencing. The framework allows participants using various call signalling protocols, such as SIP, H.323, Jabber, Q.931 or ISUP, to exchange media in a centralized unicast conference. Other than references to general functionality such as establishment and teardown, details of these call signalling protocols are outside the scope of this document.

The framework defines logical entities and naming conventions. It also outlines a set of conferencing protocols, complementary to the call signalling protocols, for building advanced conferencing applications. It is compatible with the functional model presented in the SIP Conferencing Framework.
sections.plainLanguage: The point of the framework is that the parts of a conferencing system can come from different suppliers and still work together. It fixes the names, the data and the protocols between the parts, and leaves the signalling protocols themselves to other documents.

sections.title: The Vocabulary
sections.content:
A focus is a logical entity that maintains the call signalling interface with each participating client and the conference object representing the active state. It acts as an endpoint for each of the supported signalling protocols and is responsible for all primary conference membership operations such as join, leave and update of the conference instance, and for media negotiation and maintenance.

A conference object represents a conference at a certain stage, such as a description upon creation, a reservation or activation, which a conferencing system maintains in order to describe its capabilities and to provide access to the services available for each object independently.

A media mixer is the logical entity with the capability to combine media inputs of the same type, transcode the media, and distribute the results to a single or multiple outputs. A floor is a set of data or resources associated with a conference instance, for which a participant or group of participants is granted temporary access. A floor chair is a client authorised to manage access to one floor and to grant, deny or revoke it; the floor chair does not have to be a participant in the conference.

A sidebar is a separate conference instance that only exists within the context of a parent conference instance. Its objective is to provide additional or alternate media only to specific participants. A whisper is a one-time media input to specific participants within a specific conference instance, accomplished using a sidebar; an example would be an announcement injected only to the conference chair or to a new participant joining a conference.

A role provides the context for the set of conference operations that a participant can perform. A default role, such as standard conference participant, always exists; based on system-specific authentication and authorization, a user may take on alternate roles such as conference moderator.
sections.plainLanguage: The focus is the server at the centre. The conference object is the record of everything about the conference. A mixer combines the media. A floor is a resource that one person at a time may hold, and a sidebar is a small extra conference for a few people only.

sections.title: The Logical Parts of a Conferencing System
sections.content:
A centralized conference is an association of endpoints, called conference participants, with a central endpoint, called a conference focus. The focus has direct peer relationships with the participants by maintaining a separate call signalling interface with each. Consequently, in this centralized conferencing model, the call signalling graph is always a star.

The most basic conference supported in this model would be an ad hoc, unmanaged conference, which would not necessarily require any of the functionality defined within this framework. For example, it could be supported using basic SIP signalling with a participant serving as the focus.

The system is built around a fundamental concept of the conference object, which provides the data representation of a conference during each of the various stages of a conference. A conference object is accessed via the logical functional elements with whom a conferencing client interfaces. Those elements are a conference control server, a floor control server, any number of foci, and a notification service. A conference control protocol provides the interface between a conference and media control client and the conference control server. A floor control protocol provides the interface between a floor control client and the floor control server. A call signalling protocol provides the interface between a call signalling client and a focus. A notification protocol provides the interface between the conferencing client and the notification service.

A conferencing system can support a subset of these functions, but some components are typically used by most other advanced functions, such as the notification service, which is used to correlate information such as the list of participants with their media streams between the other components.

The media graph of a conference can be centralized, decentralized, or any combination of both, and may differ per media type. In the centralized case, the media sessions are established between a media mixer controlled by the focus and each one of the participants. In the decentralized case, the media graph is a multicast or multi-unicast mesh among the participants. The concepts in this framework clearly map to a centralized media model.
sections.plainLanguage: Every participant has its own signalling session with the focus, so the signalling picture is always a star with the focus in the middle. The system also has a server for conference data, a server for floor control, and a notification service that tells everyone what changed.

sections.title: The Conference Object
sections.content:
The centralized conference data is logically represented by the conference object. The conference object holds a conference information type, which is extensible. That type contains a conference description with times and duration, membership with roles, capacity and names, signalling with protocol, direction and status, floor information, sidebars, the mixer algorithm with its inputs and outputs, and floor controls.

In a system based on this framework, the same conference object type is used for representation of a conference during different stages, such as expressing conferencing system capabilities, reserving conferencing resources, or reflecting the state of ongoing conferences. The exact XML schema of the conference object is detailed in a separate document.

There is a core set of data in the conference information that is used in any conference, independent of the specific conference media nature, such as the mixing algorithms performed or the advanced floor control applied. This core set contains the definitions representing the conference object capabilities, membership, roles, call signalling and media status relevant to different stages of the conference life-cycle. Participants with read-only access to the conference information are typically interested in this core set only.

Along with the basic data model, the realization of this framework requires a policy infrastructure. The policies manage and control access to the data, and include local, system level boundaries associated with specific data elements such as membership, and the ranges and limitations of other data elements. Conference policies collectively refer to a set of rights, permissions and limitations pertaining to operations being performed on a certain conference object.
sections.plainLanguage: The conference object is one record that changes meaning as the conference progresses: first a template, then a booking, then the live conference. It holds who is in it, what roles they have, how each is connected, what the mixer is doing and what the floors are.

sections.title: Identifiers
sections.content:
The conference identifier is a call signalling protocol-specific URI that identifies a specific conference focus and its associated conference instance. A conference factory is one method for generating a unique conference identifier, using a call signalling interface. To realize this framework, a conferencing system is required to support SIP as the default call signalling protocol; other call signalling protocols such as ISUP are optional.

The conference object identifier is a URI that uniquely identifies a conference object and is used by the conference control protocol to access and modify the conference information. A conferencing system allocates one for every conference blueprint, every conference reservation and every active conference. A user who does not have the identifier can still join a conference through general signalling mechanisms, but the identifier is required for the user to manipulate any of the conferencing data or take advantage of any of the advanced features.

The conference user identifier is a unique identifier for a user within the scope of a conferencing system. A user may have several, for example to represent different roles. It is used with the conference object identifier to identify a user, and it is required in conference control protocol requests so that the system can apply the right policies to the command. A conferencing system must be capable of allocating and distributing a user identifier during the first signalling interaction, and must assign one when a user joins by a signalling protocol if none exists.

The mapping of the conference object identifier to other protocol-specific identifiers, such as the BFCP confid, can carry sensitive information in many conferencing systems, so the system must protect that data and give it only to authorized users. The mapping of the conference user identifier to signalling-specific user identifiers requires methods for protecting and securing a user's identity.
sections.plainLanguage: Three things need names. The conference identifier is what a participant dials. The conference object identifier is what a client uses to read or change the conference's data. The conference user identifier says which person is making a request, so the right permissions can be applied.

sections.title: The Cloning Tree
sections.content:
Any conference object in a conferencing system is created by either being explicitly cloned from an existing parent object or being implicitly cloned from a default system conference blueprint. A conference blueprint is a static conference object used to describe a typical conference setting supported by the system, and it is the basis for creation of dynamic conference objects. The document uses the cloning metaphor instead of the inheritance metaphor because it more closely fits the idea of object replication, rather than a data type re-use and extension concept.

The cloning operation needs to specify whether the link between the parent and child is maintained. If no link exists, the objects become independent and the child is not affected by operations on the parent, nor subject to any limitations of the parent. Once the new object is created it is addressed by a unique conference object URI assigned by the system. By default the newly created object contains all the data existing in the parent, and it can expand the data it contains within the schema types supported by the parent, and restrict read and write access to its own objects. Unless the object is independent, it cannot modify the access restrictions imposed by the parent.

Unless the object is independent, the parent object can enforce a different policy by marking certain data elements as parent enforceable. The values of these elements cannot be changed by directly accessing the child object, nor expanded in the child alone. In the RFC's example, Parent B is created independent of Parent A and creates two child objects, Child 1 and Child 2. Any data element of Parent B can be modified, and depending on the element the changes are reflected in the children, whereas changes to Parent A do not affect Parent B.

An ad hoc conference is created by establishing a call signalling channel with a conference factory. The factory selects one of the system-supported blueprints based on the requesting client's privileges and the media lines in the Session Description Protocol body. The selected blueprint with its default values is copied into a newly created conference object, referred to as an active conference, which becomes independent from its blueprint, and a new conference object identifier, a new conference identifier and a new focus are allocated.

A sidebar is created using the same mechanisms, by cloning the parent associated with the existing conference and updating the information specific to the sidebar. It is implicitly linked to the parent conference object rather than being independent, and the system manages and enforces the parent restrictions on it, for example that no members from outside the parent conference instance can join it and that it cannot exist if the parent conference is terminated.
sections.plainLanguage: Every conference object starts as a copy of a template or of another object. A copy can be independent, in which case later changes to the original do not touch it, or it can stay linked, in which case the parent can mark certain fields as fixed and the child cannot change them. A sidebar is a linked copy with only a few members in it.

sections.title: The Conferencing Mechanisms
sections.content:
Participants interface with the focus using an appropriate call signalling protocol. They request to establish or join a conference using it. After checking the applicable policies, the focus then either accepts the request, sends a progress indication related to the status of the request, such as for a parked call while awaiting moderator approval to join, or rejects the request using the call signalling interface. During an active conference, a conference control protocol can be used to affect the conference state. For example, requests to add and delete participants are communicated to the focus and checked against the conference policies, and if approved the participants are added or deleted using the call signalling to and from the focus.

A conferencing system is responsible for implementing a conference notification service, which provides updates about the conference instance state to authorized parties, including participants. A model for notifications using SIP is defined in the SIP event notification specification. The conference user identifier and its associated role are used by the system to filter the notifications so that they contain only information that is allowed to be sent to that user.

The conference control protocol provides for data manipulation and state retrieval for the centralized conferencing data, represented by the conference object. Its details are provided in separate documents.

A floor control protocol allows an authorized client to manage access to a specific floor and to grant, deny or revoke access of other conference users to that floor. Floor control is not a mandatory mechanism for a conferencing system, but it provides advanced media input control features. A mechanism for floor control is defined in the Binary Floor Control Protocol. A client supporting floor control needs information for connecting to a floor control server, which can be retrieved through negotiation using the SDP offer and answer exchange on the signalling interface with the focus. Every floor control message must carry the conference object identifier, the conference user identifier, and a floor identifier, which maps to the confid, userid and floorid SDP attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: Four protocols do the work. Signalling gets people in and out. The control protocol changes the conference data itself. Notifications tell participants what changed. Floor control hands a shared resource, such as the right to speak, from one person to another.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
There are a wide variety of potential attacks related to conferencing, due to the natural involvement of multiple endpoints and the many, often user-invoked, capabilities provided by the conferencing system. Examples include an endpoint attempting to listen to conferences in which it is not authorized to participate, an endpoint attempting to disconnect or mute other users, and theft of service by an endpoint attempting to create conferences it is not allowed to create.

One set of issues involves securing the protocols and the associated authorization mechanisms, which should be addressed in the specifications specific to the protocols described in section 8 and in policy control. The protocols used for manipulation and retrieval of confidential information need to support a confidentiality and integrity mechanism, and similar requirements apply for the floor control protocols. It is recommended that all the protocols that interface with the conferencing system implement Transport Layer Security.

Many policy authorization decisions are based on the identity of the user or the role that a user may have, so conferencing systems typically require authentication of users. For users joining via SIP signalling or the conference control protocol, TLS is recommended. The system may also assign passwords, and in some cases additional authorization is required, such as an Interactive Voice Response system or a Personal Identification Number. A PIN is a special case of a password that is only numeric and often contains a fairly small number of bits, as few as 10 bits or 3 digits. Because a fast interface can make thousands of attempts per second, PINs are not appropriate for authorization on any interface that provides fast queries or many simultaneous queries.

The system has an idea of the identity of a user, but this does not mean it can reveal that identity to other users. A user can be hidden, so that other users cannot see they are participants, anonymous, so that others can see that a user is there but not who they are, or public, where other users can see their identity. If there are multiple anonymous users, other parties see them as independent anonymous parties and can tell how many there are.
sections.plainLanguage: Because a conference involves many people and many controls, there is a lot to abuse. The RFC asks that every protocol carrying conference data be protected with TLS, that users be authenticated, and that short numeric PINs not be used where an attacker could try them quickly.
